correctness.rationale: The source lower-bound proof gives the complete equality budget: a shortest reset must enter the critical configuration after either \(ac\) or \(c^2\), every proper merge has length at least three, and between nonfinal merges at least \(n-3\) transport letters are needed. The source's complete minimum merge list shows the only length-three candidates are \(bcc\) and \(bca\); a nonfinal \(bca\) returns the merged coin to the wrong location and costs one extra transport step, so equality forces \(bcc\) at every nonfinal merge and \(c^{n-3}\) between them. The last merge can use either minimum option, yielding exactly the displayed four words. A fresh independent power-set BFS for \(5\le n\le10\) reproduced lengths \(10,17,26,37,50,65\), exactly four shortest words, and target split \(2+2\).
correctness.risk: The universal count rests on the equality-case reading of the published lower-bound proof; finite BFS is corroborative only.

final_claim: For every integer \(n>4\), the deficiency-two automaton \(D_n\) has exactly four shortest reset words, namely \(x c (b c^{n-1})^{n-4} b c y\) with \(x,y\in\{a,c\}\); all have length \((n-2)^2+1\), two reset to state \(1\) and two to state \(4\).
limitations: The theorem concerns the specific three-letter family \(D_n\).
Finite BFS checks are not used as an infinite proof.
